thread.title: 8%+ Yields From Voya Global Option Income Funds - Voya Global Advantage and Premium Opportunity Fund (NYSE:IGA)

author: Stanford Chemist
title: 8%+ Yields From Voya Global Option Income Funds - Voya Global Advantage and Premium Opportunity Fund (NYSE:IGA)
text:
Author's note : Data in the article are from May 4, 2018.
A member recently asked me on my thoughts on Voya Global Equity Dividend and Premium Opportunity Fund ( IGD ). As we own a similar fund, the Voya Global Advantage and Premium Opportunity Fund ( IGA ) in the Tactical Income/TI-100 portfolios, I thought it would be a good idea to inspect IGD in the context of a comparison with IGA in order to understand the differences between the two global option income CEFs.
Basic statistics about the funds are shown in the table below.
Fund IGA IGD Yield [ttm] 8.14% 10.21% Baseline expense 1.02% 1.23% Inception Oct. 2005 Mar. 2005 AUM $218m $748m Leverage 0% 0% Discount -7.53% -6.87% 1-year z-score 0.0 -0.6 Avg. Volume 61k 361k Morningstar rating *** ** No. holdings 111 81 Annual turnover 98% 31% SA followers 765 3,358 (Source: Morningstar, CEFConnect)
IGD is the older of the two funds, by about 5 months, being incepted in March 2005. IGA was incepted in October of the same year.
IGD is also the larger of the two funds at $748 million AUM, whereas IGA has an AUM of $218 million. Both funds are unleveraged.
The daily average volume of IGD is 361k shares compared to 61k for IGA; both should be sufficient for the typical retail investor.
IGD has a greater follower base on Seeking Alpha (3,358 followers) compared to IGA (765 followers including yours truly).
Voya Investments is the investment adviser for both funds and is responsible for monitoring the funds' overall investment strategy and overseeing the sub-adviser. NNIP Advisors is the sub-adviser and is responsible for investing the Fund’s assets in accordance with the Fund’s investment objective and strategies. The sub-adviser in turn has two teams that manage the Fund: the Voya Global Equity Dividend Team is responsible for the equity security selection while the Voya Structured Investment Strategies Team is responsible for implementing the funds' option strategy.
IGA's baseline expense ratio of 1.02% is reasonable however IGD's baseline expense ratio of 1.23% seems to be a bit on the high side.
Objectives Let's take a look at the objectives of the two funds. Both have the same overall objective of high income with capital appreciation as a secondary objective.
Here's a side-by-side comparison of some of the main features of the two funds as stated on the fund sponsor's website.
Feature IGA IGD Target universe Invests in global equity portfolio of 100-150 stocks Invests in 80–120 global, common stocks with a history of attractive dividend yields Option strategy Sells call options on selected security indexes and/or ETFs, on an amount equal to approximately 50–100% of the value of the Fund’s common stock holdings Sells call options on selected indices and/or on individual securities and/or ETFs to seek gains and lower volatility of total returns over a market cycle Currency hedging Hedges major currency exposure to reduce volatility of returns May partially hedge currency exposure to reduce volatility of returns The first notable difference between the two funds are that IGD invests in high dividend stocks (as its fund name suggests) whereas IGA has no high dividend mandate.
Let's now take a look to see if there are any differences between the option strategy between the two funds. The following data are taken from the fund factsheets (as of March 31, 2018).
IGA
IGD
We can see that the call option statistics are nearly identical for the two funds. Both funds write index options with an option life of 51 days and a time to maturity of 22 days. Both portfolios have ~50% option coverage. The only slight difference is that IGA writes at-the-money [ATM] calls whereas IGD apparently writes both ATM and out-of-the-money [OTM] calls.
IGD also shows the currency option statistics, however, this table is not shown in the factsheet for IGA.
Portfolio Recall that IGD has a mandate to invest in stocks with "a history of attractive dividend yields" whereas IGA has no such requirement.
This difference is manifested when comparing the top 10 holdings of the two funds, although the differences were not as large as I initially predicted. For example, both funds own Microsoft ( MSFT ) (1.79% yield) and ConocoPhillips ( COP ) (1.73% yield) in their top 10 holdings. IGA owns the non-dividend-paying Alphabet ( GOOG ) but IGD does not. IGD owns Vodafone (NASDAQ: VOD ) with an attractive 4.13% yield, but it also contains other stocks as top holdings that most investors wouldn't normally associate as dividend powerhouses, such as Apple ( AAPL ) (1.42% yield) and Citibank ( C ) (1.88% yield).
Looking at the geographical allocation, both funds have United States as the top holding. IGA has slightly more U.S. exposure, at 53.33%, compared to IGD at 48.07%. However, there are interesting differences between the international components of the two funds. IGD has France as its second largest country at 12.15%, but France does not rank even among the top 10 countries of IGA! IGA's allocation to Japan, its second largest country weight at 11.13%, is also significantly larger than IGD's Japan weighting of 7.61%, which takes third place in IGD. For reference, the iShares MSCI AWCI ETF ( ACWI ) (All World Country Index) has 51.86% allocated to U.S. stocks. Let's take a closer look at the market capitalization distribution of the two CEFs. The profile of ACWI is shown as a comparison. We can see that both IGA and IGD own exclusively giant, large and medium cap stocks. However, IGD has a larger cap tilt compared to the benchmark ACWI, whereas IGA has a smaller cap tilt compared to the benchmark. For instance, IGD has 65.2% allocated to giant cap stocks compared to 39.7% for IGA and 54.4% for ACWI. However, IGA has the higher allocations to both large cap and medium cap stocks compared to either IGD or ACWI.
(Source: Stanford Chemist, Morningstar)
Turning to valuation metrics, both IGA and IGD are cheaper than the benchmark ACWI across all four metrics (P/E, P/B, P/S and P/CF), which is encouraging to see. IGA is cheaper than IGD by P/E, but more expensive by P/B, P/S and P/CF.
(Source: Stanford Chemist, Morningstar)
Distribution IGA yields 8.14%, paid quarterly. The next quarterly dividend has not yet been declared, but the next ex-date should be in the first week of July. The current quarterly dividend amount of $0.225 has been maintained since December 2016, when it was cut by -19.7% from its previous level of $0.28.
IGD yields 10.21%, paid monthly. The next monthly dividend has not yet been declared, but the next ex-date should be in the first week of June. The current monthly dividend amount of $0.061 has been maintained since December 2016, when it was cut by -19.7% from its previous level of $0.076.
IGA Dividend data by YCharts
As both funds are option income equity funds, they will utilize capital gains and return of capital [ROC] to fund a large proportion of their distribution. Therefore, NII coverage and UNII cannot be used to assess distribution safety. Instead, a rough rule of thumb is to consider the NAV returns of the fund. If the NAV return exceeds the NAV distribution rate, then it is more likely that the distribution is safety covered, and vice versa.
IGA has a 7.54% distribution rate on NAV and its 1-year NAV total return is 9.42%. Therefore, its distribution over the last year has been adequately covered by gains.
Meanwhile, IGD has a 9.52% distribution rate on NAV and its 1-year NAV total return is 4.14%. Therefore, its distribution over the last year has not been well covered by gains.
It's also important to note that neither IGA nor IGD are tax-managed. This can be seen in the distribution breakdown of the two funds in 2017. IGA's distribution in 2017 consisted of 22% income, 59% short-term capital gains [STCG] and 19% return of capital [ROC]. For IGD, the breakdown was 29% income, 29% STCG and 42% ROC. In contrast, a tax-managed fund such as Eaton Vance Tax-Managed Global Diversified Equity Income Fund ( EXG ) had 8% income and 92% ROC in 2017. Like IGA and IGD, EXG is a global option equity income CEF with about 50% U.S. allocation and 50% option coverage.
(Source: Stanford Chemist, Morningstar)
Remember that distributions from ROC are effectively tax-deferred, meaning that ROC is actually a good thing for option income equity funds. (See Building A Database of Tax-Advantaged CEFs for more information). This would suggest that IGA and IGD should be owned in a tax-deferred account, whereas in a taxable account a tax-managed fund such as EXG should be preferred.
Performance Let's now take a look at the historical performance of the funds. NAV rather than price returns are considered because the latter are also affected by changes in premium/discount valuation of the funds.
We can see from the data below that all three option income CEFs have lagged the benchmark ETF over 1, 3, and 5-year time periods. This is entirely expected because writing covered calls is a defensive strategy that provides downside protection at the expense of some upside. Of the three CEFs, IGA has performed the best over the 1, 3 and 5-year time frames, followed closely by EXG and then IGD significantly behind.
(Source: Stanford Chemist, Morningstar)
Over the 10-year time frame, IGA was the only fund to outperform the global benchmark (note that Morningstar's "World Stock" return was used rather than ACWI since the ETF is less than 10 years old). This is significant because it demonstrates that over the entire bull-bear cycle, the option income strategy does outperform buy and hold of the index as academic literature has shown. EXG would also have outperformed the benchmark before fees, but after fees it slightly underperforms. However, IGD significantly underperforms both CEFs and the benchmark.
I also wanted to illustrate the defensive nature of the option income funds by looking at NAV total returns during two down years, 2008 and 2011, and two up years 2013 and 2017.
We can see clearly that the option income CEFs provided downside protection during 2007 and 2011. However, they lagged during the strong markets of 2013 and 2017 as expected.
(Source: Stanford Chemist, Morningstar)
Taking a look at some volatility metrics, the option income funds are all less volatile than ACWI according to annualized volatility, beta, daily variation and maximum drawdown. (Note the table below shows NAV metrics as indicated by the "X" in front and after the ticker).
Ticker Annualized Volatility Beta Daily VaR (99%) Max Drawdown XIGAX 17.6% 0.79 2.6% -43.2% XIGDX 16.2% 0.70 2.4% -50.6% XEXGX 18.9% 0.85 2.8% -51.4% ACWI 21.7% 1.03 3.2% -56.3% (Source: InvestSpy. Period from 28 March 2008 - 15 March 2018).
Valuation The following table shows the current discount and z-scores for the three global option income CEFs.
Fund Discount 1-year z-score 1-year average discount 5-year average discount IGA -7.53% 0 -7.50% -8.21% IGD -6.87% -0.6 -5.88% -8.51% EXG 0.00% 1.5 -1.49% -5.99% (Source: CEFConnect)
Based on the above data, EXG is clearly the most overvalued of the three CEFs. It's trading at parity to NAV, with a +1.5 z-score, whilst the 5-year average discount is -5.99%. IGA and IGD are similarly valued, and both are cheaper than EXG.
The 5-year premium/discount history of the three CEFs is shown below. We can see large variations in the valuation of the funds over the course of their recent histories. This is exactly what we want to see as savvy CEF investors because it means that we can exploit premium/discount behavior to add in valuable points of performance to an income portfolio, as I have written about many times previously. In that vein, anyone owning EXG in a tax-deferred account should consider switching to IGA or IGD in order to lock in the "paper profit" from the discount contraction!
Closing thoughts This article presented a head-to-head comparison of two of Voya's global option income funds, IGA and IGD.
If I had to pick one of these to invest in, I would go for IGA despite the fact that it pays quarterly and its yield is 2 percentage points lower than IGD's monthly yield, for the following reasons:
IGA charges 1.02% in baseline expense, which is 21 bps cheaper than IGD (1.23%). IGA has much better historical performance than IGD, and it also outperformed the benchmark over the full 10-year cycle. I prefer IGA's smaller cap tilt vs. the benchmark compared to IGD's larger cap tilt for diversification reasons. IGA's discount is slightly wider at -7.53% vs. -6.87% for IGD, despite it having the higher z-score. This analysis also saw how EXG was slightly overvalued. If in a tax-deferred account, one could consider switching to IGA. However, IGA is not tax-managed so it may not be the best choice for a taxable account.
